title: Tazria: pray for the one outside (Leviticus 13:45–46)
hook: the afflicted cries "unclean"; the Talmud says so that others will pray for him (Shabbat 67a)

segments.voice: Yesterday the priest waited a week before deciding. Your line was look again in a week. Did one decision get a date instead of a guess? Today, the end of Tazria, and a cry from outside the camp. Day three hundred ninety-nine.

It's one of the loneliest pictures in the Torah. Someone has been declared to have tzara'at. Their clothes are torn, their hair left loose, their lip covered, the signs of a mourner. They live alone, outside the camp. And when anyone approaches, they have to call out a word. Read plainly, it sounds like a warning label: stay back. That's how many readers have heard it. The Talmud hears something else in the same cry.
screen: `TORN CLOTHES, LOOSE HAIR.` → `ALONE, OUTSIDE THE CAMP.` → `A CRY, OR A WARNING?`

segments.voice: The verses, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: the person shall cry, "Unclean, unclean." And: "he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his dwelling be." In tractate Shabbat, the rabbis ask why he has to announce it at all. Their answer: so that he makes his pain known to many, and many will ask for mercy for him. The cry isn't only keep away. It's also: I'm here, I'm suffering, remember me. That changes what the camp can do. The person outside can't come in. But the people inside can still pray, if they pray, and they can remember. The boundary stays, and the bond stays too. Jewish practice carries this forward in a prayer called the mi sheberakh for the sick, said at the Torah reading, where names of people who are ill are spoken aloud so the whole congregation holds them. Some people ask to have their own name read. In this tradition, telling others isn't weakness. It's how you let them carry you a little. And the cry closes a hard week. Aaron's sons died and Aaron grieved, first in silence, then with reasons Moses accepted. Shemini ended with kadosh, holy in the everyday. Tazria began with a birth, then tzara'at, a priest who must look, and a priest who waits. And now a person outside the camp, whose cry asks the camp to pray.
screen: `UNCLEAN, UNCLEAN.` · `SO THAT MANY WILL PRAY.` · `THE MI SHEBERAKH FOR THE SICK.` · `A WEEK OF GRIEF AND SKIN.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE ONE OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone isolated. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is outside the camp right now. Sick at home. In a hospital. Grieving alone. Far away, or cut off, or just lonely in a full house. Say their name to yourself. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for them in your own words, or with a prayer you know. If you don't, hold them in mind with care for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. The portion that ends with a person crying out from outside the camp, so that others will pray for them.

Your line: pray for the one outside. Today, if something is weighing on you, tell one person, the way the cry lets the camp know, and let them hold it with you. Day three hundred ninety-nine, and another week behind you.

howItsDone: In many synagogues, during the Torah reading, the congregation says the mi sheberakh prayer for the sick, naming people who are ill, often with their Hebrew name and their mother's name.

fork.setup: you're outside the camp with tzara'at, and someone is walking toward you. what does the Torah have you do?
fork.reveal: you cry out. and the Talmud says the point is not only warning: it's so that many will hear and pray for you.

original.note: Hebrew: "unclean, unclean": the cry of Leviticus 13:45.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning label.
what it means: a cry that lets the camp know someone is suffering, so they can pray.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 67a reads Leviticus 13:45 as making one's pain known to the many so they ask for mercy; the mi sheberakh for the sick continues the idea.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 13:45 'Unclean, unclean' and 13:46 'he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his dwelling be' quoted from memory; confirm wording and punctuation.
Shabbat 67a (also Moed Katan 5a, Niddah 66a): announcing so that many will seek mercy; confirm.
Mi sheberakh custom of using the mother's name varies; howItsDone says 'often'.

Audit (second sample): the teach's 'First... Second... Third... Fourth' scaffold (used in every day 392–421, including 398 and 400 on either side) is replaced with plain transitions; the carry's 'send a message to someone out of sight' repeated day 400's 'go out to them', so the carry now takes the Talmud's side of the cry: tell one person what you're carrying.
